main.summary: Wang Bo wrote this preface at a farewell banquet at the Pavilion of Prince Teng. He first describes the fine land and distinguished men of Hongzhou and the grandeur of the party, then the magnificent view from the pavilion; he voices his feelings as a talent unrecognised who still does not let his high ambitions fall, and ends by apologising modestly and inviting the guests to write poems. It is written in parallel prose of four and six characters, rich in ornament and wide in sweep.
main.translation:
Yuzhang was an old commandery, and Hongdu is its new prefecture. Its stars are divided by Yi and Zhen, and its land borders Mount Heng and Mount Lu. It wears the three rivers as a lapel and the five lakes as a belt; it commands the Man and Jing peoples and draws in Ou and Yue. Its products are splendid and its treasures heavenly; the glow of the dragon sword pierces the realm of the Ox and Dipper stars. Its people are outstanding and its land is blessed with spirit; Xu Ru lowered Chen Fan's couch. A mighty prefecture, spread out like mist; fine talents, speeding like stars. Its terraces and moat lie at the meeting of the Chinese and the barbarians; the guests and hosts are all the best of the southeast.

The Regional Commander, Lord Yan, of refined repute, has come from afar with his halberd banners; Governor Yuwen of Xinzhou, a model of fine conduct, has paused here for a while with his curtained carriage. It is the ten-day holiday, and fine friends are as many as the clouds. They have come a thousand li to welcome and to meet, and noble guests fill the seats. The leaping dragon and the rising phoenix are Scholar Meng, a master of the word; the purple lightning and the blue frost are General Wang, an arsenal in himself. My father is serving as a magistrate, and my road passed through this famous place. What does a boy know? Yet I have myself met a splendid farewell feast.

It is the ninth month, and the season belongs to deep autumn. The flood waters have drained and the cold pools are clear; the misty light has gathered and the evening hills are purple. I had the horses of my carriage lined up on the high road, and went looking for the scenery on the lofty hill. I came to the long isle of the prince, and found the old hall of a heavenly being. Layered peaks stand green, rising above the many heavens; flying pavilions flow with red, looking down on ground that is not there. Crane shores and duck islets take in all the windings of the isles; cassia halls and orchid palaces are built to the form of the ridges and hills. I open embroidered doors and look down on carved ridge-poles. Hills and plains stretch wide to fill the sight; rivers and marshes wind to startle the eye. Village gates cover the ground, houses where bells ring and tripods feed; boats and warships fill the ferries, with prows of green sparrow and yellow dragon. The clouds have dispersed and the rain has cleared; colour pierces through and the whole region is bright. Sunset clouds fly together with a lone wild duck; autumn water shares one colour with the long sky. Fishing boats sing at evening, their sound reaching the shore of Lake Pengli; wild geese in formation start at the cold, their cries cut off at the bank of Hengyang.

My distant heart has just opened, and a free delight flies up. A clear piping rises and a pure breeze is born; thin songs freeze and the white clouds are stopped. The green bamboo of the Sui garden: its spirit surpassed the cups of Pengze. The red blossoms of the River Ye: their light shone on the brush of Linchuan. The four beauties [a fine season, fine scenery, a glad heart and a joyful occasion] are all here, and the two hard-to-find [a worthy host and fine guests] are joined. We gazed our fill at the middle of the sky, and took our fill of pleasure on a free day.

The sky is high and the earth far; I feel the universe is without end. Joy ends and sorrow comes; I know that fullness and emptiness have their number. I look at Chang'an beneath the sun, and gaze at Wu and Kuaiji among the clouds. The lie of the land reaches its end and the southern sea is deep; the pillar of Heaven is high and the North Star far. Passes and hills are hard to cross; who grieves for the man who has lost his way? Meeting like duckweed on the water, we are all guests in a strange land. I long for the Emperor's gate and do not see it; in what year shall I attend upon him in the Xuanshi Hall? Alas! Fortune is uneven and the road of fate is crooked. Feng Tang grew old easily, and Li Guang was hard to ennoble. Jia Yi was wronged at Changsha, yet it was not that there was no sage ruler; Liang Hong was banished to a sea coast, yet was that a time that lacked brightness? What we rely on is that the noble person sees the moment and the person of wide understanding knows fate. In old age one should grow stronger - how could a white head change its heart? In poverty one should be firmer - never let the aim of reaching the blue clouds fall. Drink from the Greed Spring and still feel clear; sit in a dry rut and still be glad. The North Sea is far, yet the whirlwind can reach it; the morning corner of the sky has gone, yet the mulberry and elm of evening are not late. Mengchang was lofty and pure, yet was left only with a vain love for serving his country; Ruan Ji was wild and unrestrained, but should I copy his weeping at the end of the road?

Bo, of three-foot humble rank, a mere scholar, has no road to ask for the tassel, and is the same as Zhong Jun at his young age; I have a mind to throw down the brush, and I admire the long wind of Zong Qin. I put aside hairpin and tablet for a hundred years, to attend on my father morning and evening ten thousand li away. I am no precious tree of the Xie family, yet I am joined to fragrant neighbours like those of Mencius. Another day I shall hurry across the courtyard, humbly joining in the answer of Li; today I raise my sleeves, glad to be entrusted to the Dragon Gate. Yang Yi is not met, so I stroke my "Soaring Above the Clouds" and pity myself; Zhong Ziqi has already been met, so what shame is there in playing "Flowing Water"?

Alas! Famous places do not last, and grand feasts are hard to repeat. The Orchid Pavilion is gone, and Zize is a mound of ruins. At parting I give words, and am fortunate to have received favour at this great farewell; climbing high to write a rhapsody is what I look for from you, gentlemen. I dare to exhaust my humble thoughts and respectfully set down this short introduction. One word each, let all compose; four rhymes together are done. Let us pour out Pan's river, and each tip over Lu's sea.

keyLines.line: 物華天寶，龍光射牛斗之墟；人傑地靈，徐孺下陳蕃之榻
keyLines.en: Its products are splendid and its treasures heavenly; the glow of the dragon sword pierces the Ox and Dipper stars. Its people are outstanding and its land is blessed with spirit; Xu Ru lowered Chen Fan's couch.
keyLines.note: With the glow of a precious sword and the stories of Xu Ru and Chen Fan, he praises Hongzhou for its fine products and outstanding people.

keyLines.line: 落霞與孤鶩齊飛，秋水共長天一色
keyLines.en: Sunset clouds fly together with a lone wild duck; autumn water shares one colour with the long sky.
keyLines.note: The most famous scene in the piece: sunset glow, the lone duck, autumn water and the long sky melt into one view, motion answering stillness.

keyLines.line: 天高地迥，覺宇宙之無窮；興盡悲來，識盈虛之有數
keyLines.en: The sky is high and the earth far; I feel the universe is without end. Joy ends and sorrow comes; I know that fullness and emptiness have their number.
keyLines.note: At the height of the feast comes sorrow, and he turns to feelings about life's chances and the waxing and waning of fortune.

keyLines.line: 關山難越，誰悲失路之人；萍水相逢，盡是他鄉之客
keyLines.en: Passes and hills are hard to cross; who grieves for the man who has lost his way? Meeting like duckweed on the water, we are all guests in a strange land.
keyLines.note: He expresses the shared feeling that he and the guests present are all wanderers.

keyLines.line: 老當益壯，寧移白首之心；窮且益堅，不墜青雲之志
keyLines.en: In old age one should grow stronger - how could a white head change its heart? In poverty one should be firmer - never let the aim of reaching the blue clouds fall.
keyLines.note: He says that the poorer he becomes the firmer his ambition: a famous encouraging line.

keyLines.line: 勃，三尺微命，一介書生，無路請纓，等終軍之弱冠
keyLines.en: Bo, of three-foot humble rank, a mere scholar, has no road to ask for the tassel, and is the same as Zhong Jun in his youth.
keyLines.note: He speaks of his low standing, and by the story of Zhong Jun asking for a tassel, he voices regret at having no way to serve his country.

keyLines.line: 嗚呼！勝地不常，盛筵難再
keyLines.en: Alas! A famous place does not last; a splendid feast is hard to repeat.
keyLines.note: He sighs that a fine gathering is rare, and turns to the closing, where he asks all to write poems.

keyLines.line: 請灑潘江，各傾陸海云爾
keyLines.en: Let me ask you to pour out Pan's river and each tip over Lu's sea.
keyLines.note: The closing invites the guests to show their talent, pouring out writing as rich as the rivers and seas of Pan Yue and Lu Ji.

glossary.en: xing fen Yi Zhen - stars divided by Yi and Zhen
glossary.note: The ancients matched stars in the sky with regions on the ground; Hongzhou belongs to the zones of the two star groups Yi and Zhen.

glossary.en: Xu Ru xia Chen Fan zhi ta - Xu Ru and the couch of Chen Fan
glossary.note: The Eastern Han governor Chen Fan did not receive guests, but set up a special couch for the high-minded scholar Xu Ru.

glossary.en: can fei - horses of a carriage
glossary.note: The horses that draw a carriage; here, carriages and horses. Fei is read fei.
The Prince of Teng, Li Yuanying, a son of the first Tang emperor Gaozu.

glossary.en: Feng Tang yi lao, Li Guang nan feng - Feng Tang grows old, Li Guang is hard to enfeoff
glossary.note: In the Han, Feng Tang stayed in a low post to old age, and Li Guang won great merit in war but was never made a marquis; they stand for talent unrecognised.
A legend in Guangzhou says that anyone who drinks this spring becomes greedy; Wu Yinzhi drank from it and stayed honest.

glossary.en: sang yu fei wan - the mulberry and elm is not late
glossary.note: At sunset the light touches the tops of mulberry and elm trees, a figure for old age; it means that effort in old age is still not too late.

glossary.en: Pan jiang Lu hai - Pan's river and Lu's sea
glossary.note: The literary talent of Pan Yue and Lu Ji, as rich as rivers and seas.

main.background: Wang Bo was one of the Four Eminent Poets of the early Tang (618-907). It is said that in 675 (the second year of Shangyuan), on his way to Jiaozhi to visit his father, he passed through Hongzhou, where the governor Yan Boyu was holding a great banquet at the newly restored Pavilion of Prince Teng, and Wang Bo wrote this preface on the spot and made his name at a stroke. The pavilion stands in what is now Nanchang, Jiangxi, and was built by Li Yuanying, Prince of Teng, a son of the first Tang emperor.
